title: Higaisa
summary: Higaisa is a espionage cluster that public reporting associates with Korean Peninsula interests and that came to attention through targeted campaigns against government, diplomatic, human rights and media organisations, as well as against individuals working on North Korea related issues. The group's delivery tradecraft is the notable part: reporting describes weaponised document files that carry an embedded remote template or an external reference so that the visible document is harmless while the malicious part is fetched later, plus the use of social messaging and email lures tailored to the victim's professional interests. Analysts have also described obfuscated script loaders and the abuse of legitimate software to run the loader, which reduces the value of file-based detection and pushes defenders toward behavioural telemetry. Attribution is stated with limited to moderate confidence in public reporting, and the cluster overlaps in tooling with other tracked sets, so individual intrusions are hard to assign definitively. Evidence includes document metadata, external template fetch requests in proxy logs, unusual script interpreter invocations and command and control connections. A common misunderstanding is that a document with a clean local scan is safe; template injection means the dangerous content was never inside the file.

beginner.definition: Higaisa is a name researchers use for a group that spies on government offices, journalists and human rights workers. Public reports link it to interests on the Korean Peninsula. It mostly spreads through documents that arrive by email or chat.
beginner.whyItMatters: The document in this attack looks completely normal, and a virus scan of the file may find nothing. The harmful part is downloaded later, from the internet, when you open it. That means your protection must watch network traffic and program behaviour, not just the files you receive. These targets hold sensitive information about real people, so the harm goes beyond one office.
howItWorks: The attacker writes a document that fits the victim's work, such as a report or an invitation.
The document contains a link to a template, which is a normal feature of office software.
When the victim opens it, their computer quietly fetches a file from the attacker's server.
That fetched file runs a hidden script instead of formatting text.
The script installs a tool that gives the attacker remote control of the machine.
Defenders spot the activity in network records, not in the document itself.
beginner.example: Think of a recipe card that says see the back of the packet for cooking times. The card itself is harmless. Whoever holds the packet decides what the instructions really say, and they can change them at any time. A document that loads part of itself from the internet works the same way. The card is clean, but the instructions come from somewhere you do not control.
takeaways: A clean scan of a document does not prove it is safe, because part of it may be downloaded later.
Watch for office programs making unexpected connections to the internet.
Treat unexpected documents about your own specialism as suspicious until verified.

objectives: Explain what remote template injection is and why it defeats local file scanning.
Describe the network evidence that reveals a document fetching content from the internet.
Explain why targeted lures are built around the victim's professional interests.
Identify script interpreter activity that indicates a loader rather than normal administration.
State how public reporting qualifies attribution for this cluster.
